## The method is never the whole story

On Monday, we used disciplines to see different parts of a management problem.

Today we ask the prior question: **What assumptions lead a team to call one
kind of evidence persuasive, relevant, or sufficient?**

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3. Use a familiar contrast: a survey can
show a broad pattern; it cannot, on its own, show how every community makes
meaning of that pattern. Neither fact makes one method universally superior.
:::

## By the end of class, you can

- distinguish ontology, epistemology, methodology, and axiology;
- compare how paradigms shape questions and evidence; and
- select a defensible combination of approaches for a contested decision.

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3–7.3.3. These objectives prepare
students to identify assumptions and then use them in a management case.
:::

## A paradigm is a working worldview {.section-slide .divider-plan background-color="#123f5a"}

It shapes what a researcher takes to be real, how knowledge can be developed,
which methods fit, and what purposes should guide inquiry.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2. Make the term less intimidating:
students already make assumptions when they decide that a number, story, map,
or meeting should carry weight in a decision.
:::

## Four questions sit underneath a research design {.smaller}

| Foundation | Plain-language question |
|---|---|
| **Ontology** | What is real here? |
| **Epistemology** | What can we know, and how? |
| **Methodology** | What process can produce credible knowledge? |
| **Axiology** | What values and responsibilities guide the inquiry? |

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1.
:::

::: notes
Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1. Give a deer-management example.
One team may treat attitude as a measurable construct; another may focus on the
different meanings residents attach to deer. Both must still explain how their
approach produces credible knowledge and how it will be used.
:::

## Axiology is why “value-free” is not the whole answer

Researchers and managers make choices about:

- which problems are worth studying;
- whose experiences and knowledge are included;
- what harms to avoid; and
- how findings should be used.

Naming those choices does not make research less rigorous. It makes its
responsibilities more visible.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1. Connect to Weeks 4–5: a monitoring
system is built around objectives, and governance determines who helps set
them. Axiology is not an excuse to ignore evidence; it clarifies what evidence
is being sought and why.
:::

## The same wolf issue can generate different rigorous questions

| Starting point | A question it makes possible |
|---|---|
| Measure a pattern | What percentage of residents supports recovery? |
| Interpret meaning | How do communities describe what wolves represent? |
| Examine power | Whose voices are absent from recovery decisions? |
| Solve a problem | What evidence mix can support a workable decision? |

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2. These are adapted from the
chapter's key point. Ask students which question a statewide survey answers
best and which require a different design. Do not characterize any one question
as the “correct” starting point in all contexts.
:::

## Positivism: measure a reality that exists independently

Positivist work emphasizes observation, experimentation, and logical reasoning
to identify patterns in a reality that is “out there” to be discovered.

**Useful when:** a question calls for careful measurement of a relationship or
effect.

**Watch for:** meanings, histories, and unequal power may not be captured by
measurement alone.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.1.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.1. Use the chapter's message-test
example: Does exposure to a particular habitat-restoration message increase
support? Explain that a carefully designed experiment can be very strong for
that bounded causal question.
:::

## Post-positivism: measure carefully and stay revisable

Post-positivism still values systematic empirical inquiry, but treats knowledge
as provisional because observation, measurement, and interpretation are
imperfect.

It invites transparent limits: sampling error, uncertainty, bias, and plausible
alternative explanations.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.2.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.2. Tie this to monitoring: a survey
estimate of support for chronic-wasting-disease actions is useful, but it does
not represent every resident perfectly or eliminate the need to revisit a
decision as conditions change.
:::

## Interpretivism: examine how people make meaning {.section-slide .divider-do background-color="#2f6b57"}

People's experiences, cultures, histories, and contexts shape what a species or
management action means to them. Multiple perspectives are part of the object
of inquiry—not simply noise around one number.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3. Transition to approaches where
the goal is not a single average or one universal interpretation.
:::

## Interpretive evidence is systematic, not “just stories”

Interviews, focus groups, participant observation, and narrative analysis can
be designed carefully to examine how people construct meaning.

For wolf recovery, an interpretive study might ask how ranchers, Tribal members,
agency staff, and urban residents each describe wolves and their management.

The goal is to understand context and differences in meaning—not to force them
into a single account.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3. Connect to the Arizona and
commercial-fisher examples from Week 4: qualitative evidence can identify a
blind spot in a measurement system. Rigor comes from transparent design and
interpretation, not from pretending a lived experience is a percentage.
:::

## Critical approaches ask how power shapes knowledge

Critical inquiry examines how history, inequality, marginalization, and
disenfranchisement affect whose knowledge is treated as legitimate and who
experiences the consequences of a decision.

It carries an explicit commitment to justice, empowerment, and social change.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.4.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.4. Connect directly to Week 5: a
participation process can appear inclusive while still withholding influence.
Ask what evidence would reveal historical exclusion from a wildlife decision,
and what a team would owe people once it recognized that exclusion.
:::

## Pragmatism asks what combination can improve this decision

Pragmatism treats knowledge as a tool for addressing a problem under real
constraints: time, funding, politics, uncertainty, and implementation capacity.

It can combine survey patterns, interviews, and public testing of alternatives
when that combination is useful and credible for the decision at hand.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.5.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.5. Avoid describing pragmatism as
“anything goes.” It still requires a defensible fit between the question,
evidence, feasibility, transparency, and decision process.
:::

## Indigenous knowledge systems are not an add-on data source {.section-slide .divider-learn background-color="#123f5a"}

They are complete, place-based systems of knowledge, practice, relationship,
responsibility, and governance.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3. State this plainly before any
example. Do not collapse distinct Nations, communities, or knowledge systems
into one generic category.
:::

## Two-Eyed Seeing: work from the strengths of both eyes

**Etuaptmumk**, often translated as *Two-Eyed Seeing*, is a Mi’kmaw concept
that recognizes the value of Indigenous and Western knowledge systems while
seeking respectful, meaningful partnership.

It is not a shortcut for extracting local observations into a Western project.
It requires attention to relationships, sovereignty, and who guides the work.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3.1.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3.1. Pair this with the governance
lecture: Tribal governments are sovereign decision-makers, not simply a
stakeholder group. Emphasize that the concept names an orientation toward
respectful partnership, not a universal method that others can claim without
relationship or accountability.
:::

## Case diagnosis: choose evidence without choosing sides

**Scenario:** A state agency must revise a drought-season fishing closure. It
has creel data, temperature records, and public comments, but hears that its
current process misses subsistence and Tribal fishing perspectives.

In groups of three:

1. Name one question the agency must answer.
2. Name two kinds of evidence or knowledge that fit it.
3. State one process condition required for that evidence to be used responsibly.

::: notes
Time: 8 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3–7.3.3. Debrief toward fit and
accountability. Good answers may include biological thresholds plus community
experience, but require a process that recognizes sovereignty and does not ask
one group to validate a decision already made.
:::

## Friday

Read the **Week 06 Case Brief: Four Proposals on One Desk — The Thornapple
Lake Decision** before class. Everything you need is in it.

Four rigorous proposals, one $180,000 budget, an eight-month deadline, and a
late letter from a Tribal fisheries program setting a condition about who owns
the knowledge.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3.1–7.3.3.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3.1–7.3.3. Tell students the roles this
week are question and paradigm lead, methods and evidence lead, and standpoint
and limits lead, and that the group and role roster is already published. Warn
them that the budget arithmetic is part of the grade: Proposal 4 alone leaves
$30,000, and Proposal 3 runs a month past the deadline.
:::

## Close: rigor is a match among question, evidence, and responsibility

Paradigms make our assumptions inspectable. That is useful because management
decisions need evidence that is credible **and** a process that is appropriate
to the people, places, and consequences involved.

**Next week:** use psychology to move from “people should care more” to a
specific, observable behavior and a plausible strategy.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3–7.4.
:::

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3–7.4. Exit prompt: What assumption
about evidence do you now notice in a management claim? Use a few responses to
open the next class, then connect to Chapter 8's behavior frameworks.
:::
